greek.meaning: recognition, discovery, the moment of critical realization
greek.forms: nominative ἀναγνώρισις, genitive ἀναγνωρίσεως, dative ἀναγνωρίσει, accusative ἀναγνώρισιν
greek.etymology: From ἀνα- (again, back) + γνωρίζω (to make known, recognize), from γνώ- root of γιγνώσκω (to know). The noun form indicates the action or moment of recognizing.
greek.literary_context: Aristotle defines ἀναγνώρισις in the Poetics as a change from ignorance to knowledge, producing love or hate between persons destined for good or bad fortune, with the recognition of Oedipus being the finest example.
greek.usage_example: καλλίστη δὲ ἀναγνώρισις ὅταν ἅμα περιπετείᾳ γένηται. — The finest recognition is when it occurs simultaneously with reversal.
greek.did_you_know: Aristotle considered the anagnorisis of Oedipus discovering his true identity as king-slayer and mother-husband to be the supreme example of tragic recognition, demonstrating how knowledge can transform a man from apparent wisdom to utter ruin.

latin.etymology: From sordēs 'filth, dirt,' ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *swerd- 'dirty, black.' Related to Greek ῥύπος 'filth.'
latin.literary_context: Horace uses sordidus in Satires 1.6 to describe the low social origins from which he came, contrasting himself with aristocratic Romans who looked down on those of humble birth.
latin.usage_example: Nihil est tam sordidā avaritiae turpius. — Nothing is more contemptible than base greed.
latin.did_you_know: The word sordidus gave rise to the English word 'sordid,' but in Latin it could refer not only to moral baseness but also to the deliberate wearing of dirty clothes by Roman defendants in court to evoke pity from judges.

french.meaning: mother-of-pearl; the iridescent inner layer of certain shells
french.forms: singular: nacre; plural: nacres (though rarely used in plural)
french.etymology: From Italian naccara, naccaro, ultimately from Arabic نقارة (naqqāra) 'small drum' (shells were used to make drums). The word entered French in the 16th century.
french.literary_context: Baudelaire employs nacre in Les Fleurs du Mal to evoke precious, shimmering surfaces that contrast with decay. Verlaine also uses it in his Romances sans paroles to suggest delicate, opalescent beauty.
french.usage_example: Les coquillages révélaient leur nacre aux reflets changeants sous la lumière du matin. — The shells revealed their mother-of-pearl with shifting reflections in the morning light.
french.did_you_know: Symbolist poets prized nacre as an image of subtle beauty and transformation, since its surface changes color with the angle of light, making it a perfect emblem for the ineffable qualities they sought to capture in verse.

german.forms: die Innigkeit, gen. der Innigkeit, pl. (rare) die Innigkeiten
german.etymology: From innig (inward, heartfelt, intimate) + -keit (suffix forming abstract nouns). Innig derives from Middle High German innec, from inne (within, inside), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *innanē.
german.literary_context: Hölderlin uses Innigkeit to describe the sacred intimacy between mortals and the divine in his hymns. Novalis employs it throughout Heinrich von Ofterdingen to capture the Romantic soul's deep inward communion with nature and spirit.
german.usage_example: Die Innigkeit seiner Gebete rührte alle Anwesenden. — The heartfelt depth of his prayers moved all present.
german.did_you_know: For German Romantics, Innigkeit designated not mere sentiment but an ontological mode of being—the capacity to dwell authentically in spiritual presence, uniting subject and object in what Novalis called magical idealism.

italian.forms: singular: pietà, pietade (archaic); no plural in standard usage
italian.etymology: From Latin pietatem (accusative of pietas), meaning dutiful conduct, devotion, piety. Related to pius. The semantic shift from religious duty to compassion occurred in medieval usage.
italian.literary_context: Dante uses pietà throughout the Inferno to describe the complex emotion of compassion toward the damned, most memorably in Canto V when he faints from pietà after hearing Francesca's tale: "e caddi come corpo morto cade."
italian.usage_example: Quando rispuosi, cominciai: "Oh lasso, / quanti dolci pensier, quanto disio / menò costoro al doloroso passo!" / Poi mi rivolsi a loro e parla' io, / e cominciai: "Francesca, i tuoi martìri / a lacrimar mi fanno tristo e pio." — When I answered, I began: "Alas, what sweet thoughts, what longing led them to the grievous pass!" Then I turned to them and spoke, and began: "Francesca, your torments make me weep with sadness and pity."
italian.did_you_know: Dante's use of pietà is morally ambiguous: Virgil sometimes rebukes him for feeling compassion toward the damned, suggesting that pietà toward those justly punished might itself be a form of sin against divine justice.

oldenglish.forms: nom. scop, acc. scop, gen. scopes, dat. scope; nom. pl. scopas
oldenglish.etymology: From Proto-Germanic *skapiz, related to scieppan 'to shape, create.' The scop is literally a 'shaper' of words, cognate with Old Norse skáld and ultimately sharing a root with Modern English 'shape.'
oldenglish.literary_context: In Beowulf (lines 90-98), a scop in Heorot sings of Creation, performing the lay that provokes Grendel's rage against the joyful hall-music.
oldenglish.usage_example: Hwīlum cyninges þegn guma gilphlæden gidda gemyndig se ðe ealfela ealdgesegena worn gemunde word oþer fand soðe gebunden. Secg eft ongan sið Beowulfes snyttrum styrian ond on sped wrecan spel gerade wordum wrixlan. — Sometimes the king's thane, a man laden with proud speeches, mindful of songs, he who remembered a great many of old tales, found other words truly bound together. The man began again to set forth Beowulf's journey skillfully and to relate successfully a well-made tale, to vary his words.
oldenglish.did_you_know: The scop held a privileged position in Anglo-Saxon society, often attached to royal courts and responsible for preserving tribal history and genealogy through oral performance. Unlike the later minstrel, the scop was both composer and performer, shaping new verses in traditional formulaic style.

middleenglish.meaning: faithfulness, loyalty, integrity; a sworn pledge or promise
middleenglish.forms: singular: trouthe; plural: trouthes; genitive: trouthes
middleenglish.etymology: From Old English trēowþ 'faithfulness, truth', related to trēowe 'faithful'. Cognate with Old Norse tryggð, Gothic triggwa. The semantic range encompasses both abstract truthfulness and concrete pledges of loyalty.
middleenglish.literary_context: In Chaucer's Canterbury Tales, the Knight is described as one who 'loved chivalrie, / Trouthe and honour, fredom and curteisie,' establishing trouthe as the foundation of chivalric virtue. The Franklin's Tale turns entirely on the keeping of trouthe when Dorigen must honor her rash promise.
middleenglish.usage_example: He shal his trouthe plighte and swere to kepe his covenant. — He shall pledge his faith and swear to keep his covenant.
middleenglish.did_you_know: Trouthe is the first virtue named in the portrait of Chaucer's Knight and appears throughout medieval literature as the supreme secular virtue, ranked above even courage. When characters break their trouthe, tragedy inevitably follows, as seen in Troilus and Criseyde.

welsh.meaning: a long poem in strict meter, especially one composed for the National Eisteddfod
welsh.etymology: From Middle Welsh awdl, borrowed from Latin ōdēs (plural of ōda 'ode'), ultimately from Greek ᾠδή (ōidḗ) 'song, poem'. The term evolved in Welsh to denote specifically the elaborate formal poems composed in cynghanedd.
welsh.literary_context: Goronwy Owen's 'Awdl Foliant i Dduw' (1753) exemplifies the classical awdl form, employing intricate cynghanedd and strict metrical patterns to create a hymn of divine praise that revitalized Welsh bardic tradition in the eighteenth century.
welsh.usage_example: Enillodd y bardd gadair yr Eisteddfod am ei awdl ar thema 'Goleuni'. — The poet won the Eisteddfod chair for his awdl on the theme 'Light'.
welsh.did_you_know: The Eisteddfod's tradition of awarding a chair to the author of the best awdl dates to the medieval court poets, though the modern competitive form crystallized in the nineteenth century as Welsh cultural nationalism sought to preserve the sophisticated metrical system of cynghanedd.

oldnorse.meaning: creator, maker, shaper (especially of fate or the world)
oldnorse.forms: nom. sg. skǫpuðr; acc. skǫpuð; gen. skǫpuðs; dat. skǫpuði; nom. pl. skǫpuðar
oldnorse.etymology: From the verb skapa 'to shape, create' + agent suffix -uðr (< Proto-Germanic *-udaz). Related to Old English scieppend 'creator,' ultimately from Proto-Germanic *skapjaną 'to create.' The root *skap- carries the fundamental meaning of shaping or forming.
oldnorse.literary_context: The word appears in the Poetic Edda's Vǫluspá (stanza 4), where it refers to the gods as creators: 'Þá gengu regin ǫll á rǫkstóla, ginnheilog goð, ok um þat gættusk; nótt ok niðjum nǫfn of gáfu, morgin hétu ok miðjan dag, undorn ok aptan, árum at telja; hittusk æsir á Iðavelli, þeir er hǫrg ok hof há timbruðu, afla lǫgðu, auð smíðuðu, tangir skópu ok tól gørðu.' The term emphasizes divine creative power.
oldnorse.usage_example: Þá spurði Gangleri: 'Hverr er æðstr ok ágæztr allra goða?' Hárr segir: 'Alfǫðr heitir á váru máli, en í Ásgarði enum forna átti hann tólf nǫfn... hann er skǫpuðr himins ok jarðar.' — Then Gangleri asked: 'Which is highest and most glorious of all the gods?' The High One says: 'All-Father he is called in our tongue, but in ancient Asgard he had twelve names... he is the creator of heaven and earth.'
oldnorse.did_you_know: While Christianity brought the Latin loanword skaparinn to mean God the Creator, the pagan skǫpuðr was already deeply embedded in Norse cosmology, referring to the shaping forces behind both the world and individual human fate, reflecting the Norse belief that destiny was something woven or shaped rather than predetermined.
